screens.title: Simulating Robots with Gazebo and URDF
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how a robot’s physical body is described in URDF and how that description is used by Gazebo to simulate motion, collisions, and sensors. We begin by seeing URDF as a structured blueprint: links represent rigid parts, joints define how parts move relative to one another, and visual, collision, and inertial tags tell simulators what to render and how physics should behave. Then we connect that model to Gazebo using plugins so ROS topics such as cmd_vel can actually move the robot and odom can report its pose. You will examine a compact example URDF for a differential drive robot with two wheels, see the gazebo_ros_diff_drive plugin configured, and run a launch file that loads the model and spawns it into an empty world. Along the way we’ll point out practical tips: keep collision geometry simple for real-time physics, set sensible mass and inertia values, and test with low velocities to avoid tipping. By the end you should be able to write a minimal URDF, attach a simple plugin, launch Gazebo, and send commands to move a simulated robot — a safe, repeatable step before working on hardware. What sensor would you add to your robot first, and why?

Simulating Robots with Gazebo and URDF

Model the robot body with URDF, attach Gazebo plugins to bridge physics and ROS, then launch a simulated robot and control it through ROS topics. This workflow helps you iterate safely before deploying to hardware.

In this lesson

  • Launch the robot and test with simple velocity commands
Coming up

  • Configure differential drive plugin and spawn the model
  • Observe odometry and sensor topics
Explore Key Topics
URDF Structure
Links, joints, inertial and separate visual vs collision geometry.
Gazebo Plugins

Launch & Test

Visual Blueprint
Differential drive example
A rectangular base and two cylindrical wheels with a diff drive plugin mapped to /cmd_vel.

Gazebo uses realistic physics that can cause tipping or energetic collisions. Start with low speeds and conservative mass/inertia values, and validate sensors and controllers in simulation before moving to hardware.

screens.title: What is URDF?
screens.narratorSegment: URDF stands for Unified Robot Description Format and is an XML-based schema used to describe the physical composition of a robot for ROS and simulators. At its core, URDF defines links — rigid bodies that represent parts such as a base or a wheel — and joints that connect those links and define possible relative motion. Each link typically includes visual geometry for rendering, collision geometry for efficient physics checks, and inertial parameters describing mass and the inertia tensor needed for realistic dynamics. A practical example is a mobile base: you model the rectangular body as a link with a box visual, the wheels as cylindrical links, and joints of type continuous or revolute to allow rotation. A common misconception is to use identical, highly detailed meshes for both visual and collision geometry. That makes the model look accurate but slows down simulation; instead keep collision geometry simple and reserve detailed meshes for visual tags. Another important point is that inertial values are not optional for dynamic simulation: inaccurate mass and inertia can make the robot behave unrealistically or destabilize controllers. Think of URDF as the robot’s specification sheet; it tells Gazebo what pieces exist, how they connect, and how they should physically interact. To test your understanding, try identifying the link and joint definitions in the provided sample URDF and imagine how changing a mass value would affect the simulated motion.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › What is URDF?
Definition

URDF: the robot blueprint

URDF is an XML file that declares links, joints, and the geometry and inertial parameters required for simulation and visualization.

Key parts
  • Link: a rigid body with visual, collision, and inertial sections.
  • Joint: connects parent and child links and defines motion type.
  • Inertial: mass and inertia tensor required for physics.
Key Takeaway

URDF expresses both structure and physics. Keep collision geometry simple, and always include inertial data for dynamic simulation.

Analogy & Example
Think of URDF as a set of LEGO instructions

Each link is a brick and the joints are the hinges that let bricks rotate. The visual block makes the model look good, collision blocks tell the physics engine where to collide, and inertial data gives each brick its weight and balance.

Common misconception

Using identical complex meshes for both visual and collision is tempting, but it degrades performance. Use simplified primitives for collision whenever possible.

Check your understanding
  • Identify a link in an example URDF and point out its visual and inertial tags.

screens.title: Links: visual, collision, and inertial
screens.narratorSegment: A link in URDF is not just a shape — it contains three distinct responsibilities. The visual tag describes geometry and materials used when rendering the robot in RViz or Gazebo. This geometry can be detailed because it only affects appearance. The collision tag defines simpler geometry optimized for physics calculations; these shapes are used by the simulation engine to determine contacts and collisions in real time. Finally, the inertial tag includes mass and an inertia matrix that allows physics engines to compute forces, torques, and resulting accelerations. A good practical example is a wheel: the visual element may reference a detailed cylinder mesh for appearance, while the collision may use a basic cylinder primitive slightly simplified in size. A common mistake is to omit inertial information or use very small inertia values; the simulator will then compute unrealistic accelerations and controllers will be hard to tune. Another pitfall is placing collision geometry so it intersects other links at rest; that causes immediate collisions on spawn. When authoring a link, verify that visual and collision align and that inertial values reflect the expected mass distribution. Finally, a short check: alter the mass of the base_link and observe how easy or hard it becomes for the same torque to accelerate the robot. That is the practical meaning of inertial parameters.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Links: visual, collision, inertial
Definition

Three roles inside a link

Visual defines appearance, collision defines efficient physics shape, and inertial defines mass and inertia tensor for dynamics.
Visual
Detailed meshes for rendering in RViz and Gazebo.
Collision
Simplified primitives used by the physics engine.
Inertial
Mass and inertia values needed for realistic motion.
Common mistakes
  • Using complex meshes for collision geometry causes slow simulation.
  • Omitting inertial tags leads to unstable dynamics in Gazebo.
  • Collision shapes unintentionally intersecting other links on spawn causes immediate collisions.
Example
Wheel link
Visual: cylinder mesh. Collision: cylinder primitive. Inertial: small mass and inertia tensor.
Key Takeaway

Match visual and collision roughly, keep collision simple, and supply realistic inertial numbers for stable simulation.

screens.title: Joint types and when to use them
screens.narratorSegment: Joints in URDF define the permitted motion between a parent and child link. The five common types are fixed, revolute, continuous, prismatic, and floating. A fixed joint has no degrees of freedom and is used when two parts are rigidly attached. Revolute joints allow rotation within limits and are suitable for actuated arms where you want to constrain travel. Continuous joints rotate without limits — ideal for wheels where the joint is effectively a free-spinning axle. Prismatic joints provide linear motion, for example a sliding drawer or linear actuator. Floating joints allow six degrees of freedom and are rarely used for typical robot kinematics but can be useful when a free body model is required. A practical example: wheels usually use continuous joints so the wheel can spin indefinitely; an arm elbow uses a revolute joint with limits to avoid singular poses or collisions. A common misconception is to pick continuous for a joint that should be constrained; doing so will break angle limits and make controller logic incorrect. When selecting a joint type, consider the desired control interface and whether you will rely on joint limits. Also verify the joint axis and origin are correctly specified; an incorrect axis is a frequent source of unexpected motion. As a learner exercise, inspect the sample URDF wheel joint and imagine changing its type to revolute — what controller and limit changes would you need?

keyIdea.text: Choose joint types based on motion needed: continuous for wheels, revolute for constrained rotation, prismatic for linear motion, fixed when no motion is required.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Joint types
Joint types at a glance
Fixed
No motion
Revolute
Rotation with limits
Continuous
Unlimited rotation (wheels)
Prismatic
Linear motion
Floating
6 DOF free body
Example: wheel joint
Use a continuous joint for wheel links. Set axis to rotate about the wheel axle and ensure origin places the wheel at the correct position relative to base_link.
Misconception
Choosing continuous instead of revolute removes angle limits and can break controllers expecting bounded motion. Always match joint type to your control requirements.
Check your understanding

If you change a wheel joint to revolute with tight limits, what controller behavior would change and why? Consider continuous rotation and encoder wrapping.

screens.title: A minimal mobile robot URDF
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a minimal URDF for a differential-drive robot so you can see how the pieces fit together. The robot tag names the model. Inside, base_link is defined with visual, collision, and inertial tags. Each wheel is a separate link with its own geometry and inertia. Joints connect wheels to the base, here using continuous type for free rotation. Finally, the URDF adds a gazebo block containing a plugin configuration for a differential drive controller. This plugin maps left and right wheel joints, wheel diameter, and the commandTopic, typically cmd_vel, so velocity messages are translated into torques applied to the wheel joints and odom is published. A common confusion is whether gazebo blocks belong to URDF or to separate launch configurations — including a gazebo plugin inside the URDF is allowed and commonly used to attach plugin parameters directly to the robot model. In practice, you will copy and adapt the provided sample: ensure joint names match the plugin entries, set wheelSeparation and wheelDiameter correctly, and tune torque and updateRate for responsive behavior. After editing, load the URDF into the parameter server and spawn the robot to confirm the model appears and the wheels respond to cmd_vel. As a quick mental check, imagine increasing wheelDiameter in the plugin: how will that affect the computed linear velocity for a given wheel angular speed? That relationship is the core of converting joint rotations to robot motion in simulation and on real robots.

keyIdea.title: URDF to plugin connection
keyIdea.text: Joint names in URDF must match plugin configuration so topics and torques map to the correct actuators.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Minimal URDF
Code example
URDF snippet
Below is a shortened XML snippet showing base and wheel links, joint, and a gazebo plugin.
<?xml version="1.0"?>
<robot name="my_robot">
  <link name="base_link"> ... </link>

  <link name="right_wheel"> ... </link>
  <joint name="right_wheel_joint" type="continuous">
    <parent link="base_link" />
    <child link="right_wheel" />
    <origin xyz="0.2 -0.15 0" rpy="0 1.5708 0" />
    <axis xyz="0 0 1" />
  </joint>

  <gazebo>
    <plugin name="differential_drive_controller" filename="libgazebo_ros_diff_drive.so">
      <leftJoint>left_wheel_joint</leftJoint>
      <rightJoint>right_wheel_joint</rightJoint>
      <commandTopic>cmd_vel</commandTopic>
      <odometryTopic>odom</odometryTopic>
    </plugin>
  </gazebo>
</robot>
Explanation
  • Joint names in URDF must match plugin entries for correct mapping.
  • Origin and axis define physical placement and rotation direction of joints.
  • Plugin parameters convert cmd_vel messages into wheel torques and publish odom.
Concrete example
If wheelDiameter increases, the same motor angular speed produces greater linear speed. Tune plugin parameters accordingly.
Pro tip
Keep plugin updateRate moderate (e.g., 50 Hz) to balance responsiveness and CPU load.

screens.title: Loading URDF and launching Gazebo
screens.narratorSegment: To bring a URDF model into Gazebo you follow a repeatable launch sequence. First, set the robot_description parameter, commonly by loading the URDF textfile into that ROS parameter so other nodes can access it. Second, start Gazebo with an empty world or a chosen environment using the gazebo_ros empty_world launch file. Third, spawn the robot model into the running Gazebo instance using the spawn_model node provided by gazebo_ros; spawn_model reads the robot_description parameter and inserts the model at a chosen x, y, z pose. Finally, run robot_state_publisher to publish TF frames derived from joint states so that visualization and other nodes can compute transforms such as odom to base_link. A practical launch snippet shows a param line for robot_description, includes empty_world. launch, and starts spawn_model and robot_state_publisher. A common error is mismatched model names or forgetting the -urdf flag on spawn_model, which results in no model being loaded. Another frequent oversight is missing robot_state_publisher; without it TF frames are not published and RViz will not display the robot correctly. After launching, verify the model appears in Gazebo, then publish a small Twist to /cmd_vel to confirm the differential drive plugin responds. That sequence covers the minimal steps to get from file to a running simulated robot you can control and observe.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Launch & Spawn
Launch file example
<launch>
  <param name="robot_description" textfile="$(find my_first_robot)/urdf/my_robot.urdf" />
  <include file="$(find gazebo_ros)/launch/empty_world.launch" />
  <node pkg="gazebo_ros" type="spawn_model" name="spawn_robot"
        args="-param robot_description -urdf -model my_robot -x 0 -y 0 -z 0.1" />
  <node pkg="robot_state_publisher" type="robot_state_publisher" name="robot_state_publisher" />
</launch>
Checklist
  • robot_description param contains URDF text.
  • spawn_model uses -urdf flag and correct model name.
  • robot_state_publisher is running to publish TF frames.
Test command
rostopic pub /cmd_vel geometry_msgs/Twist "linear:
  x: 0.5
  y: 0.0
  z: 0.0
angular:
  x: 0.0
  y: 0.0
  z: 0.2"
Publish this small twist and watch the robot move forward and rotate in Gazebo.
Common error
Forgetting the -urdf flag or mismatching model names prevents the spawn node from inserting the robot into the world.

screens.title: Gazebo plugins and ROS integration
screens.narratorSegment: Gazebo plugins are shared libraries that extend the simulator with custom behavior, and the gazebo_ros collection contains plugin wrappers that map simulation features to ROS topics. A representative plugin is gazebo_ros_diff_drive which subscribes to cmd_vel and applies torques to wheel joints, while publishing odometry on odom. Sensor plugins such as gazebo_ros_laser and gazebo_ros_camera expose simulated laser and camera data on /scan and /camera/image_raw respectively. The plugin configuration is typically embedded inside a gazebo tag within the URDF so the plugin is associated with the model. Key parameters include joint names, wheel dimensions, update rates, and topic names. An important practical point is ensuring joint names in the plugin exactly match those in the URDF — a mismatch means the plugin cannot find the joint and will fail silently or log errors. Another practical tip is to tune torque and updateRate: too low torque and the robot will not move realistically; too high torque or too low update rate can destabilize the physics. A common misconception is treating plugins as purely visualization helpers; in reality they are the translator between ROS messages and the physics engine. When you add a new sensor plugin, validate that the expected ROS topic appears with rostopic list and then inspect messages with rostopic echo to confirm data format and update frequency. What plugin would you configure first for your robot and why?

Another practical tip is to tune torque and updateRate: too low torque and the robot will not move realistically; too high torque or too low update rate can destabilize the physics. A common misconception is treating plugins as purely visualization helpers; in reality they are the translator between ROS messages and the physics engine. When you add a new sensor plugin, validate that the expected ROS topic appears with rostopic list and then inspect messages with rostopic echo to confirm data format and update frequency. What plugin would you configure first for your robot and why?

keyIdea.text: Plugins act as translators: they convert ROS messages into physics actions and publish simulated sensor outputs as ROS topics.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Gazebo Plugins
How plugins connect
Plugins bridge ROS and Gazebo by subscribing and publishing to ROS topics while manipulating Gazebo joints and sensors.
Diff drive plugin
Subscribes to cmd_vel → applies torques to left and right wheel joints → publishes odom.
Sensor plugins
Camera and LiDAR plugins publish image and scan topics usable by ROS nodes and RViz.
Plugin parameters
  • leftJoint, rightJoint — exact names from URDF
  • wheelSeparation, wheelDiameter — used to compute odometry
  • commandTopic, odometryTopic — ROS topic names to use
Debug tips
Use rostopic list to confirm topics like /cmd_vel and /odom appear, and check Gazebo logs for plugin errors when joint names differ.
Concrete example
A configured diff drive plugin converts a published linear x and angular z into left and right wheel velocities and applies torque to those joints in Gazebo.

screens.title: Controlling the simulated robot
screens.narratorSegment: Controlling a simulated robot follows the same ROS messaging patterns as a real robot. You publish a geometry_msgs/Twist message to the /cmd_vel topic with linear and angular components. When the gazebo_ros_diff_drive plugin is configured, it reads cmd_vel, computes left and right wheel targets from wheel separation and diameter, and applies torques to wheel joints accordingly. The plugin also computes odometry and publishes it on /odom and broadcasts TF frames, typically odom→base_link, which other nodes use for localization and visualization. A concrete example is publishing a small forward linear x and a small angular z to make the robot move while turning. A common pitfall is publishing only raw wheel velocities when the plugin expects a Twist message; ensure your controller or test publisher uses the correct message type. Another practical issue is timing: publish at a sensible rate or use latched/one-shot commands only when appropriate; continuous control requires a steady stream of Twist messages or a controller node. To verify behavior, use rostopic echo on /odom to see position updates and run rviz or tf tools to inspect transforms. Finally, remember this flow mirrors how you would control a real differential-drive robot, which makes testing in simulation an especially valuable step before deploying code to hardware.

keyIdea.text: Publish geometry_msgs/Twist to /cmd_vel; the plugin applies forces and publishes odom/TF so other nodes can use pose information.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Controlling the Robot
Process
cmd_vel → plugin → wheels → odom
  1. Publish geometry_msgs/Twist to /cmd_vel with linear.x and angular.z.
  2. Plugin computes wheel velocities from robot geometry and commanded twist.
  3. Plugin applies torques to joints and publishes odometry on /odom.
  4. robot_state_publisher and TF broadcast the odom→base_link transform for consumers.
Test Publisher Example
rostopic pub /cmd_vel geometry_msgs/Twist "linear:
  x: 0.5
  y: 0.0
  z: 0.0
angular:
  x: 0.0
  y: 0.0
  z: 0.2"
Verify
  • rostopic echo /odom to watch position updates.
  • Use TF viewers to confirm odom→base_link transform updates.
Pitfall
Publishing at an irregular or too-low rate can lead to jerky motion; controllers expect steady update frequency.

screens.title: Sensor plugins: LiDAR and camera
screens.narratorSegment: Simulated sensors in Gazebo let you develop perception and control algorithms without physical hardware. The gazebo_ros_laser plugin provides a LiDAR simulation and publishes scan messages on a topic such as /scan. The gazebo_ros_camera plugin simulates an image sensor and publishes raw image topics like /camera/image_raw. When added to URDF, sensor plugins declare frame names, topic names, update rates, and noise or range parameters to approximate real devices. A practical lab step is to add a gazebo_ros_ray or gazebo_ros_laser plugin into the URDF and verify messages appear with rostopic list and rostopic echo. Use RViz Image and LaserScan displays to visualize data. One important caveat is that simulated sensors are idealized; they often have less noise and perfect timing compared to physical sensors. To close the gap, tune plugin noise and update parameters to mimic expected real-world behavior. A common mistake is forgetting to include the sensor frame in TF: without the proper frame transforms the data cannot be interpreted relative to the robot. Add the sensor link and ensure robot_state_publisher publishes the transform from sensor link to base_link. As a practice question, after adding a LiDAR plugin, what topic will you inspect and what will you expect to see when the robot nears an obstacle?

screens.title: How Gazebo, URDF, and ROS fit together
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the runtime architecture clarifies responsibilities and debugging steps. The URDF file is loaded into the ROS parameter server under robot_description so many nodes can read it. When you start Gazebo, the gazebo_ros package provides an empty world and a bridge for ROS connectivity. spawn_model reads robot_description and inserts the model into Gazebo. Plugins embedded in the URDF attach to the spawned model and handle actuators and sensors, subscribing and publishing to ROS topics. robot_state_publisher consumes joint states and broadcasts TF transforms like odom→base_link for visualization and other nodes. From a troubleshooting perspective, if the model is missing, check spawn_model logs and verify robot_description. If odometry or sensors are absent, inspect plugin logs and rostopic list for missing topics. If transforms are missing in RViz, confirm robot_state_publisher is running and that joint_state messages are published. The architecture creates a clean separation: URDF defines what the robot is, Gazebo simulates the physics, plugins connect simulation to ROS topics, and launcher files orchestrate the whole startup. Visualizing this chain helps you isolate errors and iterate on models and plugin parameters quickly. How Gazebo, URDF, and ROS fit together means urdf → robot_description param → spawn_model → gazebo with plugins → ros topics and tf via robot_state_publisher.. In practical terms, a practical architecture: parameter server, gazebo, plugins, spawn_model, and robot_state_publisher.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Components and responsibilities
URDF
Model definition for links, joints, visuals, collisions, and plugins.
Parameter Server
Holds robot_description so spawn_model and other nodes can access the URDF.
Gazebo
Simulates physics and hosts the spawned model and plugins.
spawn_model
Reads robot_description and inserts the model into Gazebo, setting initial pose.
robot_state_publisher

Troubleshooting guide

  • No odom: verify plugin configuration and topic names.

screens.title: Lab walkthrough: build, launch, and test
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on walkthrough guides you through the lab activity. Start by creating a URDF file named my_robot. urdf that includes a rectangular base_link and two cylindrical wheel links named left_wheel and right_wheel. Add a small caster as a third link if you like. Provide visual, collision, and inertial sections for each link, keeping collisions simple. Next, inside the URDF add gazebo plugin blocks: a differential drive plugin configured with leftJoint and rightJoint matching your joint names, wheelSeparation and wheelDiameter set to your base geometry, and topics cmd_vel and odom. For sensors, add a gazebo_ros_ray (LiDAR) plugin for the base with a topic /scan and a gazebo_ros_camera plugin for a camera link publishing /camera/image_raw. Then write a launch file robot_gazebo. launch that loads robot_description from your URDF, starts empty_world. launch, spawns the model with spawn_model, and runs robot_state_publisher. Launch the file and confirm the robot appears in Gazebo. Publish a Twist to /cmd_vel and verify the robot moves; then echo /scan and /camera/image_raw to confirm sensor output. Finally, implement a simple Python node that reads /scan, checks the closest range, and publishes a Twist: move forward when clear, otherwise rotate to avoid obstacles. Test obstacle avoidance by placing obstacles in Gazebo and observing behavior. This cycle ensures you validate model, plugin, launch, control, and perception in a single lab session.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Lab Walkthrough
Tasks
  1. Write my_robot.urdf: base_link, left_wheel, right_wheel, visual/collision/inertial.
  2. Add gazebo plugin for differential drive with matching joint names and topic mappings.
  3. Add LiDAR and camera plugins with topics /scan and /camera/image_raw and correct frames.
  4. Create robot_gazebo.launch to set robot_description, include empty_world.launch, spawn_model, and run robot_state_publisher.

  6. Implement a Python node that reads /scan and publishes /cmd_vel to avoid obstacles.
Example check

Safety step
Start with low linear and angular speeds in your Python controller. Observe behavior and tune thresholds for obstacle distance before increasing speed.
Reflection
Which sensor helped the avoidance node most, LiDAR or camera? LiDAR gives direct range readings, making simple reactive avoidance straightforward.

screens.title: Simulation vs Reality
screens.narratorSegment: Simulation is an approximation designed for repeatability and safety, not an exact replica of the real world. Gazebo models rigid body dynamics, collisions, and many sensor behaviors, but key differences remain: motors on real robots have friction, backlash, and latency; sensors have noise, distortion, and dropouts; and real environments contain unpredictable elements that are hard to model. When transitioning from simulation to hardware expect some controllers and parameters to need retuning. A practical approach is to introduce realism into the simulation: add sensor noise parameters, model expected friction, and test with slightly imperfect collisions. Also, validate assumptions such as exact wheel diameter, wheel slip, or encoder resolution because these influence odometry and localization. A common mistake is assuming a controller that works perfectly in Gazebo will immediately perform identically on a real robot; always perform low-speed tests and staging steps on hardware. Finally, simulation is invaluable for early development: it reduces risk, speeds iteration, and allows repeated testing. Use simulations to prototype architecture and algorithms, but always plan and budget time for tuning when you deploy to the physical robot. What single change would you make in your simulation to better match the expected noise profile of your real sensors?

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how a robot’s physical body is described in URDF and how that description is used by Gazebo to simulate motion, collisions, and sensors. We begin by seeing URDF as a structured blueprint: links represent rigid parts, joints define how parts move relative to one another, and visual, collision, and inertial tags tell simulators what to render and how physics should behave. Then we connect that model to Gazebo using plugins so ROS topics such as cmd_vel can actually move the robot and odom can report its pose. You will examine a compact example URDF for a differential drive robot with two wheels, see the gazebo_ros_diff_drive plugin configured, and run a launch file that loads the model and spawns it into an empty world. Along the way we’ll point out practical tips: keep collision geometry simple for real-time physics, set sensible mass and inertia values, and test with low velocities to avoid tipping. By the end you should be able to write a minimal URDF, attach a simple plugin, launch Gazebo, and send commands to move a simulated robot — a safe, repeatable step before working on hardware. What sensor would you add to your robot first, and why?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to read and write a basic URDF description, launch that robot inside Gazebo, connect Gazebo sensors and actuators to ROS topics with plugins, and control the simulated robot using standard ROS topics. First, you will understand URDF elements like link, joint, visual, collision, and inertial and why each exists. Second, you will author a minimal URDF for a mobile platform with wheels and a sensor and ensure collision shapes are simplified for efficient simulation. Third, you will configure gazebo_ros plugins — for example the differential drive plugin — so that publishing velocity commands on cmd_vel results in forces applied to wheel joints and odometry published on odom. Finally, you will run a launch file that loads the robot_description parameter, starts Gazebo, spawns the model, and brings up robot_state_publisher so TF frames are published. Each objective includes a simple practical milestone: write the file, launch the scene, publish a twist message, and observe sensor topics. These are repeatable skills that transfer to later labs and physical robots. Which milestone will you try first when you open your workspace?

This second objectives screen translates goals into a short lab checklist you can follow. First, draft a URDF file for a differential-drive robot: include a base_link and two wheel links, set visual and collision geometry, and add inertial tags with reasonable mass and inertia values. Second, extend the URDF with a gazebo plugin section for a differential drive controller configured to listen on cmd_vel and publish odometry to odom. Third, write a launch file that sets robot_description, starts an empty Gazebo world, and runs spawn_model plus robot_state_publisher. Fourth, test the simulation by publishing a Twist message on cmd_vel and checking that the robot moves and that /odom is updated. Finally, add a LiDAR plugin and a camera plugin to the URDF and confirm data appears on /scan and /camera/image_raw. Each step helps you validate a different part of the chain: model geometry, physics mapping, ROS integration, and sensor outputs. When you run these steps, keep velocities low and check collision geometry for unexpected intersections to avoid unstable physics. Which step will you run first in your lab?

URDF stands for Unified Robot Description Format and is an XML-based schema used to describe the physical composition of a robot for ROS and simulators. At its core, URDF defines links — rigid bodies that represent parts such as a base or a wheel — and joints that connect those links and define possible relative motion. Each link typically includes visual geometry for rendering, collision geometry for efficient physics checks, and inertial parameters describing mass and the inertia tensor needed for realistic dynamics. A practical example is a mobile base: you model the rectangular body as a link with a box visual, the wheels as cylindrical links, and joints of type continuous or revolute to allow rotation. A common misconception is to use identical, highly detailed meshes for both visual and collision geometry. That makes the model look accurate but slows down simulation; instead keep collision geometry simple and reserve detailed meshes for visual tags. Another important point is that inertial values are not optional for dynamic simulation: inaccurate mass and inertia can make the robot behave unrealistically or destabilize controllers. Think of URDF as the robot’s specification sheet; it tells Gazebo what pieces exist, how they connect, and how they should physically interact. To test your understanding, try identifying the link and joint definitions in the provided sample URDF and imagine how changing a mass value would affect the simulated motion.

A link in URDF is not just a shape — it contains three distinct responsibilities. The visual tag describes geometry and materials used when rendering the robot in RViz or Gazebo. This geometry can be detailed because it only affects appearance. The collision tag defines simpler geometry optimized for physics calculations; these shapes are used by the simulation engine to determine contacts and collisions in real time. Finally, the inertial tag includes mass and an inertia matrix that allows physics engines to compute forces, torques, and resulting accelerations. A good practical example is a wheel: the visual element may reference a detailed cylinder mesh for appearance, while the collision may use a basic cylinder primitive slightly simplified in size. A common mistake is to omit inertial information or use very small inertia values; the simulator will then compute unrealistic accelerations and controllers will be hard to tune. Another pitfall is placing collision geometry so it intersects other links at rest; that causes immediate collisions on spawn. When authoring a link, verify that visual and collision align and that inertial values reflect the expected mass distribution. Finally, a short check: alter the mass of the base_link and observe how easy or hard it becomes for the same torque to accelerate the robot. That is the practical meaning of inertial parameters.

Joints in URDF define the permitted motion between a parent and child link. The five common types are fixed, revolute, continuous, prismatic, and floating. A fixed joint has no degrees of freedom and is used when two parts are rigidly attached. Revolute joints allow rotation within limits and are suitable for actuated arms where you want to constrain travel. Continuous joints rotate without limits — ideal for wheels where the joint is effectively a free-spinning axle. Prismatic joints provide linear motion, for example a sliding drawer or linear actuator. Floating joints allow six degrees of freedom and are rarely used for typical robot kinematics but can be useful when a free body model is required. A practical example: wheels usually use continuous joints so the wheel can spin indefinitely; an arm elbow uses a revolute joint with limits to avoid singular poses or collisions. A common misconception is to pick continuous for a joint that should be constrained; doing so will break angle limits and make controller logic incorrect. When selecting a joint type, consider the desired control interface and whether you will rely on joint limits. Also verify the joint axis and origin are correctly specified; an incorrect axis is a frequent source of unexpected motion. As a learner exercise, inspect the sample URDF wheel joint and imagine changing its type to revolute — what controller and limit changes would you need?

Let's walk through a minimal URDF for a differential-drive robot so you can see how the pieces fit together. The robot tag names the model. Inside, base_link is defined with visual, collision, and inertial tags. Each wheel is a separate link with its own geometry and inertia. Joints connect wheels to the base, here using continuous type for free rotation. Finally, the URDF adds a gazebo block containing a plugin configuration for a differential drive controller. This plugin maps left and right wheel joints, wheel diameter, and the commandTopic, typically cmd_vel, so velocity messages are translated into torques applied to the wheel joints and odom is published. A common confusion is whether gazebo blocks belong to URDF or to separate launch configurations — including a gazebo plugin inside the URDF is allowed and commonly used to attach plugin parameters directly to the robot model. In practice, you will copy and adapt the provided sample: ensure joint names match the plugin entries, set wheelSeparation and wheelDiameter correctly, and tune torque and updateRate for responsive behavior. After editing, load the URDF into the parameter server and spawn the robot to confirm the model appears and the wheels respond to cmd_vel. As a quick mental check, imagine increasing wheelDiameter in the plugin: how will that affect the computed linear velocity for a given wheel angular speed? That relationship is the core of converting joint rotations to robot motion in simulation and on real robots.

To bring a URDF model into Gazebo you follow a repeatable launch sequence. First, set the robot_description parameter, commonly by loading the URDF textfile into that ROS parameter so other nodes can access it. Second, start Gazebo with an empty world or a chosen environment using the gazebo_ros empty_world launch file. Third, spawn the robot model into the running Gazebo instance using the spawn_model node provided by gazebo_ros; spawn_model reads the robot_description parameter and inserts the model at a chosen x, y, z pose. Finally, run robot_state_publisher to publish TF frames derived from joint states so that visualization and other nodes can compute transforms such as odom to base_link. A practical launch snippet shows a param line for robot_description, includes empty_world. launch, and starts spawn_model and robot_state_publisher. A common error is mismatched model names or forgetting the -urdf flag on spawn_model, which results in no model being loaded. Another frequent oversight is missing robot_state_publisher; without it TF frames are not published and RViz will not display the robot correctly. After launching, verify the model appears in Gazebo, then publish a small Twist to /cmd_vel to confirm the differential drive plugin responds. That sequence covers the minimal steps to get from file to a running simulated robot you can control and observe.

Gazebo plugins are shared libraries that extend the simulator with custom behavior, and the gazebo_ros collection contains plugin wrappers that map simulation features to ROS topics. A representative plugin is gazebo_ros_diff_drive which subscribes to cmd_vel and applies torques to wheel joints, while publishing odometry on odom. Sensor plugins such as gazebo_ros_laser and gazebo_ros_camera expose simulated laser and camera data on /scan and /camera/image_raw respectively. The plugin configuration is typically embedded inside a gazebo tag within the URDF so the plugin is associated with the model. Key parameters include joint names, wheel dimensions, update rates, and topic names. An important practical point is ensuring joint names in the plugin exactly match those in the URDF — a mismatch means the plugin cannot find the joint and will fail silently or log errors. Another practical tip is to tune torque and updateRate: too low torque and the robot will not move realistically; too high torque or too low update rate can destabilize the physics. A common misconception is treating plugins as purely visualization helpers; in reality they are the translator between ROS messages and the physics engine. When you add a new sensor plugin, validate that the expected ROS topic appears with rostopic list and then inspect messages with rostopic echo to confirm data format and update frequency. What plugin would you configure first for your robot and why?

Controlling a simulated robot follows the same ROS messaging patterns as a real robot. You publish a geometry_msgs/Twist message to the /cmd_vel topic with linear and angular components. When the gazebo_ros_diff_drive plugin is configured, it reads cmd_vel, computes left and right wheel targets from wheel separation and diameter, and applies torques to wheel joints accordingly. The plugin also computes odometry and publishes it on /odom and broadcasts TF frames, typically odom→base_link, which other nodes use for localization and visualization. A concrete example is publishing a small forward linear x and a small angular z to make the robot move while turning. A common pitfall is publishing only raw wheel velocities when the plugin expects a Twist message; ensure your controller or test publisher uses the correct message type. Another practical issue is timing: publish at a sensible rate or use latched/one-shot commands only when appropriate; continuous control requires a steady stream of Twist messages or a controller node. To verify behavior, use rostopic echo on /odom to see position updates and run rviz or tf tools to inspect transforms. Finally, remember this flow mirrors how you would control a real differential-drive robot, which makes testing in simulation an especially valuable step before deploying code to hardware.

Simulated sensors in Gazebo let you develop perception and control algorithms without physical hardware. The gazebo_ros_laser plugin provides a LiDAR simulation and publishes scan messages on a topic such as /scan. The gazebo_ros_camera plugin simulates an image sensor and publishes raw image topics like /camera/image_raw. When added to URDF, sensor plugins declare frame names, topic names, update rates, and noise or range parameters to approximate real devices. A practical lab step is to add a gazebo_ros_ray or gazebo_ros_laser plugin into the URDF and verify messages appear with rostopic list and rostopic echo. Use RViz Image and LaserScan displays to visualize data. One important caveat is that simulated sensors are idealized; they often have less noise and perfect timing compared to physical sensors. To close the gap, tune plugin noise and update parameters to mimic expected real-world behavior. A common mistake is forgetting to include the sensor frame in TF: without the proper frame transforms the data cannot be interpreted relative to the robot. Add the sensor link and ensure robot_state_publisher publishes the transform from sensor link to base_link. As a practice question, after adding a LiDAR plugin, what topic will you inspect and what will you expect to see when the robot nears an obstacle?

Understanding the runtime architecture clarifies responsibilities and debugging steps. The URDF file is loaded into the ROS parameter server under robot_description so many nodes can read it. When you start Gazebo, the gazebo_ros package provides an empty world and a bridge for ROS connectivity. spawn_model reads robot_description and inserts the model into Gazebo. Plugins embedded in the URDF attach to the spawned model and handle actuators and sensors, subscribing and publishing to ROS topics. robot_state_publisher consumes joint states and broadcasts TF transforms like odom→base_link for visualization and other nodes. From a troubleshooting perspective, if the model is missing, check spawn_model logs and verify robot_description. If odometry or sensors are absent, inspect plugin logs and rostopic list for missing topics. If transforms are missing in RViz, confirm robot_state_publisher is running and that joint_state messages are published. The architecture creates a clean separation: URDF defines what the robot is, Gazebo simulates the physics, plugins connect simulation to ROS topics, and launcher files orchestrate the whole startup. Visualizing this chain helps you isolate errors and iterate on models and plugin parameters quickly. How Gazebo, URDF, and ROS fit together means urdf → robot_description param → spawn_model → gazebo with plugins → ros topics and tf via robot_state_publisher.. In practical terms, a practical architecture: parameter server, gazebo, plugins, spawn_model, and robot_state_publisher.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. This hands-on walkthrough guides you through the lab activity. Start by creating a URDF file named my_robot. urdf that includes a rectangular base_link and two cylindrical wheel links named left_wheel and right_wheel. Add a small caster as a third link if you like. Provide visual, collision, and inertial sections for each link, keeping collisions simple. Next, inside the URDF add gazebo plugin blocks: a differential drive plugin configured with leftJoint and rightJoint matching your joint names, wheelSeparation and wheelDiameter set to your base geometry, and topics cmd_vel and odom. For sensors, add a gazebo_ros_ray (LiDAR) plugin for the base with a topic /scan and a gazebo_ros_camera plugin for a camera link publishing /camera/image_raw. Then write a launch file robot_gazebo. launch that loads robot_description from your URDF, starts empty_world. launch, spawns the model with spawn_model, and runs robot_state_publisher. Launch the file and confirm the robot appears in Gazebo. Publish a Twist to /cmd_vel and verify the robot moves; then echo /scan and /camera/image_raw to confirm sensor output. Finally, implement a simple Python node that reads /scan, checks the closest range, and publishes a Twist: move forward when clear, otherwise rotate to avoid obstacles. Test obstacle avoidance by placing obstacles in Gazebo and observing behavior. This cycle ensures you validate model, plugin, launch, control, and perception in a single lab session.

Simulation is an approximation designed for repeatability and safety, not an exact replica of the real world. Gazebo models rigid body dynamics, collisions, and many sensor behaviors, but key differences remain: motors on real robots have friction, backlash, and latency; sensors have noise, distortion, and dropouts; and real environments contain unpredictable elements that are hard to model. When transitioning from simulation to hardware expect some controllers and parameters to need retuning. A practical approach is to introduce realism into the simulation: add sensor noise parameters, model expected friction, and test with slightly imperfect collisions. Also, validate assumptions such as exact wheel diameter, wheel slip, or encoder resolution because these influence odometry and localization. A common mistake is assuming a controller that works perfectly in Gazebo will immediately perform identically on a real robot; always perform low-speed tests and staging steps on hardware. Finally, simulation is invaluable for early development: it reduces risk, speeds iteration, and allows repeated testing. Use simulations to prototype architecture and algorithms, but always plan and budget time for tuning when you deploy to the physical robot. Let’s summarize the essential ideas you should retain. First, URDF is the robot description: links, joints, visual, collision, and inertial elements describe both appearance and physics. Second, Gazebo plugins act as translators between ROS topics and the simulator, for example mapping cmd_vel into wheel torques and publishing odometry on odom. Third, the practical workflow is write URDF, load it into robot_description, start Gazebo, spawn the model, run robot_state_publisher, and then test by publishing Twist messages and inspecting sensor topics. Remember to keep collision geometry simple, include realistic inertial values, and tune plugin parameters carefully. As you move toward hardware, add noise models and friction into simulation and plan for retuning when deploying.
